## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 2: Study design](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/data-design.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn the difference between a population and a sample, how simple random, stratified, and convenience samples behave, and what separates a randomized experiment from an observational study.

### Exercise 1

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `study-design`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it. You may need to restart this tutorial after you do so.

Create a new file, `analysis.qmd`, with the title `"Study Design"` and your name as the author. In a bash Terminal, render it:

```bash
quarto render analysis.qmd
```

Open `analysis.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes on every render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Create a `.gitignore` with `analysis_files` followed by a blank line. Commit and push. Use AI however you like.

If `show_file()` fails, it is probably because you have not yet loaded `library(learnr2)` in the R Terminal.

```{r}
#| label: introduction-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file(".gitignore"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{.output}
analysis_files
```

###

"Before digging into the details of working with data, we stop to think about how data come to be." The question this chapter asks of every dataset is, "How were these observations collected?"

## Sampling principles and strategies

"The first step in conducting research is to identify topics or questions that are to be investigated." Ours: what was the average salary of a Major League Baseball player in 2010? For once, we have the whole population, so we can watch how samples of it behave.

### Exercise 1

Add a chunk that prints `mlb`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: sampling-principles-and-strategies-1
#| echo: false

```

###

```{r}
#| label: sampling-principles-and-strategies-1-test
#| echo: true
mlb
```

###

Each of the 828 rows is one player on a 2010 Major League roster. "Collecting data for an entire population is called a census," and that is what this data frame is.

###

The mean salary of the whole population, about $3.28 million, is a **population parameter**: a number "calculated or considered for calculation on the entire population." Usually we cannot compute it, because we have only a sample.

The Yankees averaged $8.25 million per player, the Pirates $1.29 million. The book says "some teams have a lot more money (up to 4 times as much!)," and this table shows the gap is even wider.

### Exercise 6

Start a new chunk that draws a simple random sample of 120 players from `mlb`, stores it as `mlb_srs`, and prints it. Set the random seed to 42 first, so that the same sample is drawn every time you render. Render.

```{r}
#| label: sampling-principles-and-strategies-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sampling-principles-and-strategies-6-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(42)
mlb_srs <- mlb |>
  slice_sample(n = 120)

mlb_srs
```

###

"The most basic random sample is called a simple random sample and is equivalent to drawing names out of a hat to select cases." Your 120 players may differ from ours if your code drew the sample differently, which is fine.

### Exercise 7

Replace the line that prints `mlb_srs` with one that calculates its mean `salary`. Render.

```{r}

```

###

```{r}
#| label: sampling-principles-and-strategies-7-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(42)
mlb_srs <- mlb |>
  slice_sample(n = 120)

mlb_srs |>
  summarize(mean_salary = mean(salary))
```

###

Our sample mean, about $3.29 million, is a **sample statistic**, a number "calculated on a sample of data." It lands close to the population parameter of $3.28 million, but a different sample would give a different number.

### Exercise 12

Start a new chunk that draws a stratified sample, 4 players from each `team`, stores it as `mlb_strat`, and calculates its mean `salary`. Set the random seed to 42 first. Render.

```{r}
#| label: sampling-principles-and-strategies-12
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sampling-principles-and-strategies-12-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(42)
mlb_strat <- mlb |>
  slice_sample(n = 4, by = team)

mlb_strat |>
  summarize(mean_salary = mean(salary))
```

###

"Stratified sampling is a divide-and-conquer sampling strategy. The population is divided into groups called strata," here the 30 teams, and a simple random sample is drawn within each one.

The table is sorted by team, so the first 120 rows are Arizona, Atlanta, Baltimore, Boston, and a few Cubs, and the Red Sox payroll pushes the mean up to $4.35 million. This is a **convenience sample**, "where individuals who are easily accessible are more likely to be included in the sample."

### Exercise 14

Replace the code in that chunk with a bar chart of the mean `salary` for each `team`, with teams sorted by mean salary, and a vertical line at the mean salary of the whole population. Render.


Only 13 of the 30 teams sit above the population mean, because a few very expensive rosters pull the average up. Stratifying by team guarantees every roster, rich or poor, is represented.

###

The chapter also describes cluster and multistage samples, which pick whole groups: "we break up the population into many groups, called clusters," then keep every case in a few chosen clusters. Those work best when "there is a lot of case-to-case variability within a cluster but the clusters themselves do not look very different from one another."

## Experiments and observational studies

"Studies where the researchers assign treatments to cases are called experiments." The chapter's other kind of study, where "no treatment has been explicitly applied," is observational. This section looks at one of each, starting with the stent study from Hello Data.

### Exercise 1

Start a new chunk that counts the patients in each `group` of `stent30`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-1-test
#| echo: true
stent30 |>
  count(group)
```

###

A coin flip, not a doctor, put 224 patients in the treatment group and 227 in the control group. "Researchers randomize patients into treatment groups to account for variables that cannot be controlled," and "randomizing patients into the treatment or control group helps even out such differences."

### Exercise 2

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question("In the R Terminal, run ?stent30. Copy and paste the Description and the Source.", type = "reflection")
```

###

```{.output}
Description:

     An experiment that studies effectiveness of stents in treating
     patients at risk of stroke with some unexpected results. 'stent30'
     represents the results 30 days after stroke and 'stent365'
     represents the results 365 days after stroke.

Source:

     Chimowitz MI, Lynn MJ, Derdeyn CP, et al. 2011. Stenting versus
     Aggressive Medical Therapy for Intracranial Arterial Stenosis.
     New England Journal of Medicine 365:993-1003.
```

###

"The researchers assigned the patients into their treatment groups, so this study was an experiment." The Source's title shows what the control group received, aggressive medical therapy rather than nothing, because "in medical experiments, typically the control group must get the current standard of care."

### Exercise 3

Replace the code in that chunk so that it calculates, for each `group`, the proportion of patients who had a stroke. Render.

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-3-test
#| echo: true
stent30 |>
  summarize(prop_stroke = mean(outcome == "stroke"),
            .by = group)
```

###

Within 30 days, 14.7% of the treatment group had a stroke, against 5.7% of the control group, and every patient knew which group they were in. The chapter warns of "an emotional effect of (not) taking the drug, which is difficult to quantify," which is why "researchers do not want patients to know which group they are in."

### Exercise 4

The study also recorded outcomes a year after enrollment, in `stent365`. Replace the code in that chunk so that it stacks `stent30` and `stent365` into one tibble named `stent`, with a `time` column recording `"30 days"` or `"365 days"`, and then calculates the proportion who had a stroke for each combination of `time` and `group`, as you did in Hello Data. Render.

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-4-test
#| echo: true
stent <- bind_rows(`30 days` = stent30, `365 days` = stent365, .id = "time")

stent |>
  summarize(prop_stroke = mean(outcome == "stroke"),
            .by = c(time, group))
```

###

The only way to blind this study would have been a sham surgery, where "the patient does undergo surgery, but the patient does not receive the full treatment, though they will still get a placebo effect." The chapter explains why that is a hard call: "a sham surgery tends to create additional risk, while withholding a treatment only maintains a person's risk."

### Exercise 5

Replace the summary in that chunk with a bar chart of the proportion of patients who had a stroke at each `time`, with the two groups' bars side by side. Render.

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-5-test
#| echo: true
stent |>
  summarize(prop_stroke = mean(outcome == "stroke"),
            .by = c(time, group)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = prop_stroke, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge")
```

###

The treatment bar is taller at both times, and with more than 200 patients behind each bar the gap is hard to dismiss. "In a single study, we replicate by collecting a sufficiently large sample," and "at a minimum we want to have multiple subjects (experimental units) per treatment group."

### Exercise 6

Improve the bar chart. Label each bar with its percentage, show the y-axis as percentages, and add a title, axis labels, a legend title, a subtitle that states the main finding, and a caption giving the number of patients and the source. Render.

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-6-test
#| echo: true
stent |>
  summarize(prop_stroke = mean(outcome == "stroke"),
            .by = c(time, group)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = prop_stroke, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(prop_stroke)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(title = "Stroke Rates in the Stent Experiment",
       subtitle = "Random assignment made the groups alike, so the extra strokes point to the stent",
       x = "Time Since Enrollment",
       y = "Patients Who Had a Stroke",
       fill = "Group",
       caption = "451 patients randomly assigned; Chimowitz et al. (2011)")
```

###

"Making causal conclusions based on experiments is often reasonable, since we can randomly assign the explanatory variable(s), i.e., the treatments." Even so, "randomized experiments have long been considered to be the gold standard for data collection, but they do not ensure an unbiased perspective into the cause-and-effect relationship in all cases," and an unblinded surgery is one such case.

### Exercise 9

Replace the code in that chunk so that it calculates the mean `homeownership` and the mean `multi_unit` for each value of `metro`, ignoring missing values. Render.

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: experiments-and-observational-studies-9-test
#| echo: true
county |>
  drop_na(metro) |>
  summarize(homeownership = mean(homeownership, na.rm = TRUE),
            multi_unit = mean(multi_unit, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = metro)
```

###

Metro counties have more multi-unit housing and lower homeownership, so `metro` is tied to both variables at once. "A confounding variable is one that is associated with both the explanatory and response variables."

```{r}
  labs(title = "Homeownership and Multi-Unit Housing in US Counties",
       subtitle = "Metro counties have more apartments and less ownership, so density may explain the link",
       x = "Housing Units in Multi-Unit Structures (%)",
       y = "Homeownership Rate (%)",
       color = "Metro Area",
       caption = "3,139 US counties with known metro status")
```

###

"While one method to justify making causal conclusions from observational studies is to exhaust the search for confounding variables, there is no guarantee that all confounding variables can be examined or measured." Density is one candidate; there could be others.

###

Observational studies come in two forms. "A prospective study identifies individuals and collects information as events unfold," like the Nurses' Health Study, while "retrospective studies collect data after events have taken place," as the county data does.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 2: Study design](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/data-design.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned the difference between a population and a sample, how simple random, stratified, and convenience samples behave, and what separates a randomized experiment from an observational study.

The chapter's own summary, in the authors' words:

> A proficient analyst will have a good sense of the types of data they are working with and how to visualize the data in order to gain a complete understanding of the variables. Equally important, however, is the data source. In this chapter, we have discussed randomized experiments and taking good, random, representative samples from a population. When we discuss inferential methods (starting in [Chapter 11]), the conclusions that can be drawn will be dependent on how the data were collected. [The chapter's closing figure] summarizes how sampling and assignment methods relate to the scope of inference. Regularly revisiting [that figure] will be important when making conclusions from a given data analysis.

For the stent study itself, read the original [article](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1105335) by Chimowitz and colleagues in the *New England Journal of Medicine*. For how sampling and random assignment together decide what a study can conclude, revisit the chapter's [closing figure](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/data-design.html#fig-randsampValloc).

````{verbatim}
```{r}
mlb |>
  summarize(mean_salary = mean(salary), .by = team) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_salary, y = fct_reorder(team, mean_salary))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(mlb$salary), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1 / 1000, suffix = "M")) +
  labs(title = "Mean Player Salary by Team, 2010",
       subtitle = "The Yankees paid six times what the Pirates did, so team is a natural stratum",
       x = "Mean Salary",
       y = NULL,
       caption = "828 players; USA Today salary database")
```

```{r}
stent <- bind_rows(`30 days` = stent30, `365 days` = stent365, .id = "time")

stent |>
  summarize(prop_stroke = mean(outcome == "stroke"),
            .by = c(time, group)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = prop_stroke, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(prop_stroke)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(title = "Stroke Rates in the Stent Experiment",
       subtitle = "Random assignment made the groups alike, so the extra strokes point to the stent",
       x = "Time Since Enrollment",
       y = "Patients Who Had a Stroke",
       fill = "Group",
       caption = "451 patients randomly assigned; Chimowitz et al. (2011)")
```

```{r}
county |>
  drop_na(metro) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = multi_unit, y = homeownership, color = metro)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(title = "Homeownership and Multi-Unit Housing in US Counties",
       subtitle = "Metro counties have more apartments and less ownership, so density may explain the link",
       x = "Housing Units in Multi-Unit Structures (%)",
       y = "Homeownership Rate (%)",
       color = "Metro Area",
       caption = "3,139 US counties with known metro status")
```
````

###

The page holds the chapter's two halves: how a sample relates to its population, and how an experiment differs from an observational study. "Both representative (ideally random) sampling and experiments (random assignment of treatments) are important for how statistical conclusions can be made on populations."
